work.scope: Fictional shared-reading pilot proposal. No venue, staffing, permissions, funding or real participant results are confirmed.

pages.title: A small pilot, a clear decision.
pages.lead: Propose a limited exploration of a shared reading session before making a larger commitment. The decision sought is whether to develop a properly reviewed pilot plan, not whether to open a service immediately.
pages.body: The fictional sponsor wants to understand how a common text might support discussion. This charter names the question, the conditions for proceeding and the evidence that would inform a later decision. It supplies no real venue or participant commitments.

pages.title: Name the problem to investigate.
pages.lead: Separate the proposed learning problem from a claim about demand. The premise is that a reading group might benefit from a more focused conversation; no local need has been measured.
pages.body: Write the current uncertainty as a question: under what conditions would a shared extract help participants refer to the same material? A real proposal would attach the relevant contextual source rather than treat an attractive room image as evidence.

pages.title: Make the pilot hypothesis testable.
pages.lead: A pilot hypothesis links a proposed activity with an observable signal. Keep the signal narrow enough to distinguish the question being explored from a broad promise of success.
pages.body: Example hypothesis: a common extract may make references easier to locate. A possible signal is whether an agreed observation record can identify the passages being discussed. This would not by itself establish learning, satisfaction or a causal effect.

pages.title: Draw the scope boundary.
pages.lead: Define what the pilot includes, excludes and leaves for later review. Scope is most useful when the excluded work is as visible as the preferred activity.
pages.body: The fictional scope includes developing a discussion prompt and a proposed observation form. It excludes venue operation, recruitment, data collection and purchase commitments. Any real pilot would need its own appropriate approvals and participant arrangements.

pages.title: Describe a reversible trial.
pages.lead: Outline how the idea could be explored without implying that a real event has been scheduled. A reversible trial should leave room to stop, change the question or choose a less demanding alternative.
pages.body: Start with a paper walkthrough of an invented discussion. Review the prompt and observation fields before considering an actual session. A real session is a separate decision and cannot be authorised by this example charter.

pages.title: Put a reviewer at each gate.
pages.lead: A stage gate combines a question, a review artifact and a role that would need to confirm responsibility. Naming a role in a template does not appoint a person.
pages.body: Gate one checks whether the question is clear. Gate two checks whether the proposed method and context are suitable. Gate three asks whether the available evidence supports continuing, changing or stopping. Record actual appointments outside the fictional example.

pages.title: Expose resource assumptions.
pages.lead: List resource categories without turning unknowns into invented prices. A short pilot can still depend on preparation, facilitation, suitable materials, a setting and appropriate review.
pages.body: For each category, distinguish an available resource from an assumption and an unresolved requirement. A borrowed room shown in an illustration is not an available venue. Keep missing categories visible instead of using a single unsupported total.

pages.title: Agree when to pause.
pages.lead: Stopping conditions protect the usefulness of the pilot. Identify conditions that should trigger a pause before interpreting a disappointing signal as a reason to expand the work.
pages.body: Examples include an unclear question, an unsuitable observation method or an unresolved permission. These are review conditions, not a safety checklist or a substitute for specialist assessment. Record who can decide to resume the work.

pages.title: Plan the evidence handoff.
pages.lead: Describe the artifact that a later reviewer would receive and what it could support. The evaluation plan should keep observations, interpretations and unresolved questions separate.
pages.body: A useful handoff might include the question, versioned prompt, method limitations and an anonymised summary if real collection were separately authorised. This proposal itself provides no real records, participant information or evaluation results.

pages.title: Ask for a bounded response.
pages.lead: Close with a response form that distinguishes agreement to investigate from approval to operate. A clear request makes it possible to revise the charter without treating a polite discussion as a commitment.
pages.body: Offer the options develop the plan, revise the question or park the idea. Record the reasoning and any prerequisite source. Keep the scope note, version and unresolved responsibilities attached when this document is shared.
